doc.title: Hank Cicalo interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, April 30, 2022

title: Studio clock and old-line company producers
summary: Hank says time pressure is the producer's job, contrasting company producers at Capitol and RCA, who aimed for three tunes a session, with Lou Adler's patience.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: Were you subject to the clock? In other words if a record company had a certain budget for this artist were you feeling like well we’ve spent four hours today and we’ve got one tune down, this thing has to speed up? Or was that not your — was that more on the producer to make that call?

That’s not my job. If you’re working with a producer that’s his job. I mean if you run over because he’s screwing around with a tune that he doesn’t really like anyway you’ve got a problem. I mean you could take a three hour date and work on one tune. You know? If you’re working on an album you could spend a day on one tune or if the producer feels this might be the single or whatever. You want more control over it, you want to deal with it more, you know, it just depends on the act and the producers. Some producers, the older producers, the guys that were really old time, guys that worked at Capitol and RCA © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-

I mean by old producers I mean guys who were musicians to begin with, they were steady guys, they worked for RCA or Columbia or whatever, they were company oriented. They had so much to do in a date and they would try to make — if there were three tunes a date we did three tunes a date. It depends on the artist. I mean you can’t stifle, I’ve seen it happen boy and that’s the worst thing in the world, where you get a producer to say, “All right come on let’s go. Hurry up.” I never felt you ever got them to perform. I worked with Lou Adler, you know, who really produced so many great records, and if things in the studio were not happening quite well and you know they’re close, he would let them develop up there. He wouldn’t be on the button right away, “Let’s do a take now.” Lou would make sure that everything out there was comfortable and he made me make sure, you know. “How are the phones, Hank? Make sure the phones are all right.” Good producers will do that.
